# Demand Planning for Retail Suppliers: How To Build a More Reliable Forecast


By[Jacqueline Nance](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/profile/jacqueline-nance-sps) , *Senior Content Marketing Manager*


Last Updated November 24, 2026


8 min read


In this article, learn about:


-


- Why a supplier selling into retail forecasts both shopper sales and retailer orders


How to prepare retailer data and measure forecast error and bias


What to add to your plan that sales history can’t show


How[connected sales and inventory data](https://www.spscommerce.com/products/analytics/) supports a forecast you can trust


Demand planning for a retail supplier is a bit like being a produce vendor who tries to predict a restaurant’s order by counting the diners through the window. The diners matter, but the kitchen also orders around what is already in the walk-in cooler, the weekend special, and the size of the case. Retail works the same way: shoppers buy at the retailer’s registers, yet the supplier is paid for what the retailer orders, and those two numbers don’t always move together.


Orders passed up a supply chain can vary more than the sales behind them, a pattern described in[research on the bullwhip effect](https://www.gsb.stanford.edu/faculty-research/publications/information-distortion-supply-chain-bullwhip-effect) . That gap is why a supplier ends up forecasting two things at once: what shoppers will buy and what the retailer will order.


A reliable forecast depends more on a weekly routine than on a clever model. Each week, the supplier pulls fresh retailer sales and inventory data, compares last week’s forecast with both the sales and the orders that actually arrived, and adjusts the plan for what the retailer’s own forecast can’t see.


## What Are the Two Forecasts a Retail Supplier Manages?


A supplier selling into retail works with two forecasts that answer different questions. The sell-through forecast estimates what shoppers will buy. The retailer order forecast estimates what the retailer will order from the supplier, which depends on the retailer’s own replenishment forecast and on the inventory it already holds. Under collaborative planning, forecasting, and replenishment (CPFR), retailers and manufacturers agree on joint sales and order forecasts.

Retailer point-of-sale (POS) data and inventory positions

POS data shows the first forecast clearly and the second only partly. A[2014 study](https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/ejores/v232y2014i3p593-600.html) found a long-run balance between orders and POS data, and a method that combined order history with POS data outperformed methods using only order or POS data, by up to 125 percent by the authors' measure, in one consumable category.


More data does not always bring a better forecast, though. In a[2025 study of four consumer goods manufacturers](https://www.emerald.com/ijopm/article/45/11/1910/1275038/Revisiting-the-value-of-data-sharing-in-retail) , adding retail POS data raised accuracy by 2 percentage points at most, did not raise it at two of the four, and helped mainly around promotions and assortment changes. Its authors concluded that the larger payoff was aligned planning between supplier and retailer.


## Why Does Forecast Accuracy Start With the Data?


Three problems in retailer data can undermine a forecast before any model runs.


1. **Retailer files arrive in different formats:**[Leatherman](https://www.spscommerce.com/resources/leatherman-analytics-case-study/) , a sporting goods supplier, once waited days for retailer POS files. The files came in varied formats, and its sales teams then spent several days decoding them and running calculations by hand.[Clarks](https://www.spscommerce.com/resources/clarks-case-study) now combines data from all of its channels, so it no longer reconciles mismatched formats and reporting schedules by hand.


2. **Stockouts hide real demand** : A[study of censored demand](https://eprints.lancs.ac.uk/id/eprint/138007) used data from a large European retailer. It notes that sales can’t record demand above available supply. Sales during a stockout therefore understate what shoppers wanted, and a forecast built on that history inherits the gap.


3. **Pack sizes and item mapping break comparisons** : A 12-pack at one retailer and a 24-pack of the same item at another can look like unrelated products in a sales file. The SPS Commerce[demand planning guide](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/demand-planning) advises grouping similar products, accounting for pack-size variations, and checking data consistency before forecasting.


## How Do You Measure Forecast Reliability?


Reliability takes two measures, because a forecast can miss in size and it can miss in direction.


Volume-weighted error shows how far off the forecast was across the whole portfolio. Research on forecast evaluation describes[weighted absolute percentage error](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9718476) as total absolute error divided by total actuals, so a fast seller counts for more than a slow one.


Bias shows the direction of the misses. It is signed, so over-forecasts and under-forecasts offset each other, and a forecast can be fairly accurate while still running high or low week after week. Total forecast minus total actuals, divided by total actuals, gives the bias as a percentage.


Level and lag keep the comparison honest. The supplier measures every forecast at the same level (item, retailer and week) and at the same lag (the forecast as it stood a fixed number of weeks ahead), so that a good week at one level does not hide a poor one at another.


## What Should a Supplier Add, That Sales History Can’t Show?


Sales history describes the past. Several inputs describe what is about to change, and the supplier has to add them by hand:


-


- Promotions and features: The 2025 study found that retail POS data helped mainly around promotions and assortment changes, so a planned event belongs in the forecast as its own line, not as noise in the baseline.


New items: A new item has no sales history to project, so the plan needs a launch assumption that the supplier revisits once real sales arrive.


Lead times and pipeline: One manufacturer in the 2025 study worked with a lead time of 100 days, which puts the order decision more than three months ahead of the shelf.


Each of these adjustments gets a written reason, which turns the next error review into a lesson instead of an argument.


## How Do Suppliers Reconcile With the Retailer Each Week?


The forecast improves when both sides look at the same numbers.[Clarks](https://www.spscommerce.com/resources/clarks-case-study) used the same POS data as its retailers, and the conversation shifted from whose data was right to what action to take.


Replenishment targets belong in that conversation too. SPS Commerce guidance on[pulling replenishment reports in Walmart](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/finding-root-causes-of-replenishment-issues) advises Walmart suppliers to agree on weeks-of-supply targets with Walmart’s replenishment team. The 2025 study went a step further and proposed that retailers regularly share their replenishment forecasts with suppliers.


## What Does a Weekly Demand Planning Routine Look Like?


A weekly routine keeps the work small enough to finish:


1. Pull the latest retailer sales and inventory data and check the files for gaps and mismatched pack sizes.


2. Compute volume-weighted error and bias at the same level and lag as last week.


3. Adjust the plan for promotions, new items, and lead times.


4. Reconcile the adjusted plan with the retailer’s replenishment or category contact.


5. Record every override and its reason, so next week’s review starts from facts.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### What is the difference between demand forecasting and demand planning?


Demand forecasting estimates how much customers will buy. Demand planning uses that estimate to decide what inventory, production and replenishment the business needs. The SPS Commerce article on[demand forecasting vs. demand planning](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/demand-forecasting-vs-demand-planning-key-differences) covers the differences in more detail.


### How often should a supplier review forecast error?


The SPS Commerce guide to[collaborative planning, forecasting, and replenishment](https://www.spscommerce.com/community/articles/what-is-cpfr-collaborative-planning-forecasting-and-replenishment) points to a weekly or daily review. For most suppliers, a weekly review matches the rhythm of retailer data.


### What does forecast bias tell you that error does not?


Error shows the size of the miss, and bias shows its direction. A forecast can be fairly accurate and still run consistently high, which quietly builds excess inventory, or consistently low, which leads to stockouts.
